clinicalPearls: Characterised by short stature with delayed bone age, a distinctive face and marked expressive language delay
The face shows a triangular shape, deep-set eyes, long eyelashes, a broad prominent nose with a low-hanging columella and a wide mouth with thin lips
Expressive language is disproportionately impaired relative to comprehension and overall cognition
Intellectual ability ranges from normal to mild or moderate impairment
Delayed skeletal maturation, small hands and brachydactyly, and sometimes coeliac disease or renal anomalies occur
Caused by de novo heterozygous variants clustered in a specific region of SRCAP, encoding a chromatin-remodelling (SNF2-related) transcriptional coactivator, inherited autosomal dominantly
The name derives from the two hospitals where early cases were described, not from any clinical feature
reference.pathophysiology: SRCAP encodes a SNF2-family ATPase that acts as a chromatin-remodelling transcriptional coactivator, notably catalysing deposition of the histone variant H2A.Z into nucleosomes and serving as a coactivator for CREB-binding protein. Pathogenic variants cluster in a specific region and are thought to produce a truncated protein with a dominant effect, dysregulating the chromatin-dependent transcription of developmental genes. This disturbance affects growth, skeletal maturation and the neural circuits underlying expressive language, producing the characteristic short stature, facies and speech profile. It shares mechanistic overlap with other chromatin-remodelling and histone-modification developmental disorders.
additionalDifferentials: Other short-stature syndromes with delayed bone age
additionalInvestigations: Speech and language and developmental evaluation
Renal ultrasound and coeliac screening where indicated
Skeletal survey for brachydactyly and other changes
Targeted SRCAP sequencing or a gene panel or exome sequencing
redFlags: Significant growth failure requiring endocrine evaluation
Renal tract anomalies with functional impact
Feeding or gastrointestinal complications such as coeliac disease
reference.prognosis: Most individuals have a good general outlook with normal to mildly impaired intellect; short stature and expressive language difficulty persist and benefit from ongoing speech and educational support. Care is supportive with growth and organ surveillance.
pitfalls: Attributing the language delay to a primary hearing or environmental cause
Confusing the phenotype with Silver-Russell or Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome without gene testing
Overlooking renal anomalies or coeliac disease
Assuming intellectual disability is always present
management: Intensive speech and language therapy targeting the disproportionate expressive language delay, with augmentative and alternative communication as needed
Developmental and educational support tailored to individual cognitive ability
Growth monitoring with endocrine assessment of delayed bone age and consideration of growth-hormone evaluation
Screening for and management of associated coeliac disease with a gluten-free diet, and surveillance for renal anomalies
Dental and skeletal assessment with management of brachydactyly and orthodontic issues
Genetic counselling with SRCAP testing; variants are typically de novo so recurrence risk to parents is low, but germline mosaicism should be discussed
